column2: Therefore, fearful, one should act as if unafraid, and distrusting, as if trusting; knowing the weight of tasks, one should practise no falsehood.
Thus have I told you this tale, Yudhishthira; having heard it, conduct yourself properly among your friends.
Having grasped the highest wisdom, the difference between enemies and friends, the time for peace and war, and the means of release in calamity,
in a task common to enemies, having made an alliance with a stronger one, one should meet him with method; having gained the end, one should not trust him.
This policy, Yudhishthira, is not opposed to the three aims of life; rise up from this hearing, and delight your subjects all the more.
And let your journey be together with brahmanas, Pandava; for brahmanas are the highest good, in heaven and here, Bharata.
They are knowers of dharma, ever grateful, lord, honoured, doers of good deeds, ruler of men, by their earlier conquests.
Kingdom is the highest good, king; you will gain glory and fame, and the continuance of your family, in due order and as is just.
Of these two, Bharata, the peace and war, the well-spoken lesson made by special intelligence, a king should always, having considered it, apply it among the circle of enemies, king.
[Yudhishthira said:] "From trust, king, the greatest fear arises for a king; how then, without trusting, can a king conquer his enemies, lord of the earth?
Cut this doubt of mine; my mind is bewildered, grandsire, having heard this discourse on distrust."
[Bhishma said:] "Hear, Kaunteya, what took place in the house of Brahmadatta, the dialogue of King Brahmadatta with Pujani.
At Kampilya, in Brahmadatta's inner apartments, there lived for a long time a she-bird named Pujani.
She understood the cries of all beings, like the jivajivaka bird; omniscient and a knower of all dharma, though born in an animal womb.
She bore there one radiant son, and at the same time a son was born to the king by his queen.
Going to the seashore she brought back two fruits, for the nourishment of her own son and of the prince.
She gave one fruit to her son and the other to the prince; like the taste of nectar, it increased strength and vigour; and the prince attained great growth from eating the fruit.
Then, king, the bird, bringing a fruit, came back, and saw her son lying dead on the ground, killed by that boy.
With a face full of tears, wretched, seeing her son slain, Pujani, burning with grief, weeping, spoke.
'There is no alliance with a kshatriya, neither affection nor friendship; they associate for a reason, and abandon when their ends are gained.
No trust should be placed in kshatriyas, who injure everyone; having done harm, they soothe uselessly.
I shall now do to him a fitting vengeance, to this ungrateful, cruel, grievous betrayer of trust.
One grown up together, and eating together, and one who has come for refuge: to slay such is a threefold sin.'
Having said this, Pujani pierced the prince's eyes with her claws, and then, settled, spoke these words.
'Sin done by one's own will draws near at once; for those who have taken vengeance, their good and ill do not perish.
If a sin of action is not found in him, it is brought down upon his sons, if not on his grandsons and sons' sons.'
[Brahmadatta said:] 'Something was done by us, and something was done in return by you; both are made equal; stay, Pujani, do not go.'
[Pujani said:] 'For one who has once committed an offence, to linger on there, the wise do not praise; withdrawal there is better.
When conciliation is offered by a king with whom enmity has been made, one should not trust it; the fool is soon bound, for enmity is not stilled.
Enmity made between each other passes to sons and grandsons; when sons and grandsons are destroyed, it passes to the next world.
For all who have made enmity, distrust brings happiness; one should never trust fully one who has betrayed trust.
One should not trust the untrustworthy, and even the trusted one should not be trusted; one may freely make others trust, but should not trust others.
Mother and father are the best of kinsmen; a wife is old age; a son is mere seed; a brother is an enemy, a friend has moist hands; the self alone knows its own pleasure and pain.
Between those who have made enmity with each other there is no peace; and that reason for which I stayed has passed.
The heart of a creature once honoured with wealth and respect, who had formerly done harm, becomes distrustful; the former deed frightens him by force.
Where honour came first and dishonour afterward, a brave man should leave that dwelling, being honoured and then dishonoured.
I lived in your house a long time unharmed; now this enmity has arisen; stay happy, I shall go.'
[Brahmadatta said:] 'If one repays him for what he did, he does not offend thereby; he becomes free of debt; stay, Pujani, do not go.'
[Pujani said:] 'Friendship is not joined again between the one who has been wronged and the doer; the heart knows, of the doer and of the one wronged.'
[Brahmadatta said:] 'Friendship is joined again between the wronged and the doer; the stilling of enmity is seen, and one does not incur the sin again.'
[Pujani said:] 'There is no enmity once begun that is gone; one should not rest easy thinking "I have been soothed"; the foolish are slain through trust, so staying out of sight is better.
Those who cannot be overcome by force, even by sharpened weapons, are held by conciliation, like elephants by she-elephants.'
[Brahmadatta said:] 'From living together affection is born, even among those who end each other's lives; and mutual trust, as of a dog with a dog-eater.
For those who have made enmity with each other, enmity softened by living together does not remain, like water on a lotus leaf.'
[Pujani said:] 'Enmity has five sources, and the wise know them: that made by a woman, that born of property, that born of words, that of rivalry, and that born of offence.
In such a case the giver of the injury is to be slain, especially by a kshatriya, openly or secretly, having reckoned place, strength and the rest.
Where enmity has been made, no trust should be placed, even in a friend; enmity stays hidden, like a concealed fire in wood.
Not by wealth, nor harsh words, nor conciliation, nor sacred hearing is the fire of enmity quenched, king, like the Aurva fire in the ocean.
The fire of enmity that has risen, or a deed born of offence, does not subside without burning, king, short of the destruction of one side.
For one who was honoured with wealth and respect yet had formerly done harm, there is neither peace nor trust; the deed frightens him by force.
I did no wrong to you at all, nor you to me; I lived here before in trust; now I do not trust.'
[Brahmadatta said:] 'By time a deed is done, and so too the various acts; by time alone they proceed; who here offends whom?
Death and birth proceed equally for both; one is made to act by time, and lives by that cause.
Some are killed all at once, others one by one; time burns the pure ones, as fire reaches fuel.
I am no authority, nor are you, in the doing of good to each other; time ever brings pleasure and pain to embodied beings.
So stay here with affection, unharmed, as the time allows; what was done I forgive, and you too forgive, Pujani.'
[Pujani said:] 'If time is your authority, then enmity would exist for no one; why then do kinsmen seek requital when a kinsman is slain?
Why did the gods and asuras strike each other of old, if departure, pleasure and pain, being and non-being come by time?
Why do physicians wish to make medicine for the sick, if they ripen by time? What use is medicine?
Why do people, struck down by grief, make great lamentation? If time is your authority, why is there dharma in doers?
Your son killed my offspring, and was harmed by me; next, king, I must be bound by you.
I have done a sin against your son through grief for my son, and you must strike at me; hear my reasoning.
Men want birds for food or for play; there is no third contact; apart from killing and binding, forgiveness is fitting.
Some, from fear of killing and binding, have gone to the way of liberation; the knowers of dharma call the sorrow born of death and calamity.
Life is dear to everyone, sons are dear to everyone; everyone is alarmed by pain, and everyone wishes happiness.
Old age is sorrow, Brahmadatta; reversal of fortune is sorrow; living with the unwished is sorrow, and sorrow is born of parting from the wished.
Sorrow made by the bonds of enmity, born of violence and made by a woman: sorrow ever turns about from pleasure, and from people.
Some foolish ones say there is no sorrow in others' sorrow; he who does not know sorrow prattles in a great assembly.
But how could one who grieves, afflicted with pain, venture to speak? One who knows the taste of all sorrow knows it in others as in himself.
What was done by me to you, king, and by you to me, cannot be undone in hundreds of years, scourge of foes.
What each did to the other leaves no room for peace between us; remembering your son again and again, new enmity will arise.
He who wants to make affection while living near enmity finds no mending, like a broken clay pot.
Distrust, which brings happiness, has been settled by the knowers of artha-shastra; and Ushanas once spoke two verses to Prahlada.
Those who trust enemies, whether truthful or not, are slain in their trust, like honey by dry grass.
For enmities do not subside in families even to the tenth generation, and there are always tellers of them, if a man exists in the family.
Kings embrace their enmities and soothe, and then crush him, like a full pot against a stone.
One should never trust, king, anyone against whom one has done wrong here; having harmed others, one meets sorrow through trust.'
[Brahmadatta said:] 'Without trust, the deserving do not gather, nor do they strive at all; from fear of one or the other they are ever as if dead.'
[Pujani said:] 'He whose feet are sore and who runs on them is worn down, though he runs very carefully guarded.
He who with sore eyes looks into the wind will surely have severe pain in his eyes from the wind.
He who through delusion takes a bad road, not knowing his own strength, has his life end there.
The man who ploughs a field not knowing the rain, lacking human effort, never gets a crop.
And he who always takes food that is bitter or astringent, though lacking taste, if it is wholesome, is fit for immortality.
A man who, after wholesome food, eats other food from greed, not knowing the result, has his life end there.
Fate and human effort stand supported by each other; for the high-minded action is the instrument; the weak worship fate.
Action for one's own good must be done, sharp or mild; but the man who shuns action is always seized by misfortunes and left with nothing.
Therefore even when the outcome is doubtful, effort must be made; even abandoning everything, men should do what is for their good.
Learning, valour, skill, strength and fortitude, these five, the wise call innate friends, by which they live here.
House, goods, field, wife and well-wishers: these are called acquired; a man finds them anywhere.
The wise man delights everywhere and shines everywhere; he frightens no one, and being frightened, does not fear.
For the intelligent man, wealth, even if small, ever grows; by skill he does his work, by restraint he stands firm.
Of men of little wit, bound by attachment to the home, a bad wife devours their substance (the verse is obscure in the source text).
House, fields, friends, my own country, say others; so men sink when their reason is reversed.
One should leave a land that is afflicted, oppressed by disease and famine, and go to live elsewhere, or live where one is always honoured.
Therefore I shall go elsewhere; I cannot stay here; this deed of your son, king, cannot be undone.
A bad wife, a bad son, a bad king, a bad friend, a bad connection and a bad country, one should avoid from afar.
In a bad friend there is no trust; in a bad wife, where is delight? In a bad kingdom there is no ease; in a bad country one cannot live.
With a bad friend, ever unsteady in friendship, there is no union; in a bad connection there is contempt, and reversal of fortune.
She is a wife who speaks kindly; he is a son in whom there is joy; that is a friend in whom there is trust; that is a country where one can live.
He is a king of harsh rule where there is compulsion by force; and there is no connection with one who wishes to be poor.
Wife, country, friends, sons, relatives and kinsmen: all this belongs to a king who is virtuous and whose guide is dharma.
The subjects of a king ignorant of dharma go to ruin for lack of restraint; a king, careful and protecting, is the root of the three aims.
Having taken a sixth part as tribute, he should apply that tribute; a king who does not protect his subjects well is a thief.
The king who himself gives assurance of safety and does not make it good properly gets sin from all the world; with an unrighteous mind he goes to hell.
The king who, having given assurance, always makes it good, protecting his subjects by dharma, is to be known as the maker of all happiness.
Father, mother, teacher, protector, fire, Vaishravana and Yama: these seven qualities of a king, Manu the lord of creatures has declared.
For a king is the father of the realm, and merciful to his subjects; when he is falsely led, man goes to an animal birth.
He honours like a mother, approaches the distressed, burns the unwanted like fire, and restraining, becomes Yama.
He lets go wealth toward the desired like Kubera the giver of wishes; as a teacher by teaching dharma, and as protector by guarding.
The king who pleases townspeople and country-folk by his virtues does not lose his kingdom, since he keeps to virtue and dharma.
Knowing for himself the doings of townspeople and country-folk, that king rejoices happily in this world and the next.
He whose subjects are ever agitated, oppressed by the burden of taxes, and ruined by misfortunes, goes to defeat.
The king whose subjects flourish like a great lotus in a lake shares in the fruit of all sacrifices and is honoured in the world.
War with the strong, king, is in no way praised; for one at war with the strong, where is kingdom, where happiness?'"
[Bhishma said:] "Having spoken thus, the she-bird, taking leave of King Brahmadatta, went to the direction she wished.
This is what was said by Brahmadatta with Pujani, told by me, best of the Bharatas; what else do you wish to hear?"
[Bhishma said:] "Well, I shall tell you the policy for calamities, Bharata: how a king should act in time, even setting aside compassion.
Here too they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of Bharadvaja with the king Shatrutapa.
The king Shatrutapa, great chariot-warrior of the Sauviras, approached Kanika and asked about the determination of ends.
'How may one desire what is not yet gained, how is the gained increased, how should the increased be protected, and how the protected be applied?'
Asked for the settled meaning, the brahmana, who had determined the matter, spoke these words, reasoned and apt in reply.
'One should ever have the rod raised, ever display manliness, be without flaw, yet see the flaws of others, and follow their weak points.
People are greatly alarmed by one who ever has the rod raised; therefore one should restrain all beings by the rod alone.
So indeed the wise who see the truth praise it; therefore among the four, the rod is called chief.
When the root of a support is cut, all who live by it are destroyed; how could branches remain when the tree's root is cut?
The wise man should cut the root of the enemy's side first; then he should pursue the allies and the whole party.
Good counsel, good valour, good fighting and good flight, he should practise at the times of calamity, without hesitating.
He should be humble in word alone, while at heart like a razor; speaking gently at first, he should avoid desire and anger.
In a task shared with a rival, having made an alliance, one should not trust; the shrewd man, his work done, should quickly withdraw.
An enemy in the form of a friend he should soothe with conciliation alone, and always be wary of him, as of a snake that has entered the house.
One whose understanding is slighted should be soothed with the past; the dull-witted with the future; the wise with the present.
With folded hands, oaths, conciliation, bowing with the head, and even shedding tears, one desiring prosperity should act.
He should carry the enemy on his shoulder until the time turns; then, when the time comes, he should break him like a pot on a stone.
Even for a moment, king of kings, let one blaze like a brand of tinduka wood; a man should not smoulder long like a husk-fire without flame.
One should not deal in wealth with the useless and ungrateful; wealth can be enjoyed, but one whose task is done despises you; therefore make all tasks leave something remaining.
Of the cuckoo, the boar, Meru, the empty house, the beast of prey, and the painted pattern, whatever is best, one should take up.
Rising again and again, ever diligent, one should go to the enemy's houses and ask after his welfare, even if all is not well.
The idle do not gain wealth, nor the weak, nor the proud, nor those afraid of public talk, nor those who always wait.
Let the enemy not know his weak point, but let him know the enemy's; let him hide his limbs like a tortoise, and guard his own opening.
Let him ponder matters like a heron, strike like a lion, snatch like a wolf, and spring like a hare.
Drink, dice, women, hunting, and song and music: these one should use with moderation, for attachment to them has fault.
One should make a bow of reeds, lie down like a deer, be blind at the time of blindness, and even resort to deafness.
The shrewd man, having reached the right place and time, should show valour; for valour past place and time is fruitless.
Having weighed right and wrong time, his own strength and weakness, and knowing each side's strength, he should engage himself accordingly.
The king who does not restrain an enemy who has come under the rod embraces death, as a mule her foetus.
Let him be richly flowering yet fruitless, or fruitful yet hard to climb; raw yet seeming ripe, and yet not crumbling for anyone.
Let him make his hope last long, and join it with obstruction; let him state the obstruction by a pretext, and the pretext by a reason.
One should make provision as if afraid while the danger has not come; but seeing the danger arrived, strike like one unafraid.
A man does not see good things without taking up a risk; but having taken the risk, if he lives, he sees them.
One should foresee what has not come, restrain the danger that has come, and again consider what has come about from growth and decay.'"
But it was not done by you, Partha, nor indeed by Duryodhana; know that it was done by Time, by whom kings are ordained.
By deed, mind and speech, by self-control and calm, that lord of the earth won the hearts of his subjects.
I see nothing to be done in return against them, delight of the Kurus; all of them, slain facing the enemy, have gone to the worlds won by weapons.
Then all of them together, driven by the turn of time, the Bhojas and Andhakas, great king, surrounded Shaineya.

[Indra said:] "Abandoning your brothers and your beloved Krishna, you reached this world by your own deed, hero; how then do you not abandon this dog? Having taken up complete renunciation, you are deluded now."
Thus addressed by the wise son of Pandu, the messenger then went to where Indra, king of the gods, the lord of a hundred sacrifices, was.
